analysis.one_liner: Tightens lobbying disclosure, bars lobbyist gifts and travel, and restricts the congressional revolving door.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 396–22 on May 24, 2007, but the Senate never brought it to a vote; the bill died on the Senate calendar, while the Senate's own companion lobbying-reform bill became law that September.
analysis.plain_summary: This House bill would force Members of Congress and senior staff to disclose job negotiations with potential future employers and step aside from conflicting matters. It would require lobbyists to file quarterly, electronically, in a free searchable public database, and to report the money they bundle for politicians. It would bar registered lobbyists from providing gifts or travel not allowed under House or Senate rules, raise fines for hiding lobbying activity, and add criminal penalties for members who use official acts to influence private hiring.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and citizens, who get to see in a free searchable database who is lobbying whom, how much they are paid, which earmarks they request, and whose campaign money lobbyists bundle. Honest members and staff also gain clearer rules and written notice of the post-employment restrictions that apply to them.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Members, Delegates, and senior House staff to disclose within three business days any negotiations for future employment, and to recuse themselves from matters where a conflict exists, with the disclosure posted publicly.

Moves lobbying reports from semiannual paper filings to quarterly electronic filings, posted free on the internet within 48 hours, and doubles the civil fine for knowing violations to $100,000 with up to five years' imprisonment for knowing and corrupt violations.

Requires registered lobbyists who bundle more than $5,000 in campaign contributions for a federal candidate or officeholder in a quarter to report it, and to notify the recipient by certified mail beforehand.

Makes it a crime punishable by up to 15 years for a Member or congressional employee to take or withhold an official act in order to influence a private entity's employment decision on the basis of partisan political affiliation.

Bars registered lobbyists and lobbying organizations from providing gifts or travel to members, officers, and employees if the gift or travel could not be accepted under chamber rules, and requires lobbying reports to certify compliance.

Requires lobbying reports to disclose requests for congressional earmarks, and posts members' travel and financial disclosure reports on the Clerk's public website in a searchable, downloadable format.

analysis.who_pays: Registered lobbyists and lobbying firms, which face quarterly electronic filing, bundling disclosure, a gift-and-travel prohibition, doubled fines and new criminal penalties. Law firms with contracts to Congress and former members and senior staff face new revolving-door restrictions, and taxpayers fund the public database.

drawbacks.text: The new criminal provision threatening up to 15 years for taking an official act to influence a private employer's hiring on partisan grounds could chill ordinary constituent and political work, which is why the bill itself includes a rule of construction protecting First Amendment activity.

Lower registration thresholds and coalition-disclosure rules push compliance costs onto smaller organizations and nonprofits that engage in any lobbying, including tax-exempt associations that must now untangle who counts as the client.

Posting members' travel and financial disclosure reports online risks exposing personal information, which the bill tries to blunt by letting members omit home addresses, Social Security numbers, bank accounts, and children's names before posting.
Barring staff from any official contact with a member's lobbyist spouse intrudes into members' personal and family arrangements in the name of avoiding influence-peddling.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance the transparency gains outweigh the burdens: quarterly public disclosure of who is lobbying whom, and of the money lobbyists bundle for lawmakers, gives citizens information they previously could not easily get, while the compliance costs fall on a small, well-resourced industry. The main honest caveats are the unusually heavy 15-year penalty, which could chill legitimate political activity, and privacy risks from posting disclosure records online, which the bill partially addresses.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 396–22, the Senate read it twice and placed it on its calendar in June 2007, and it sat there until the Congress ended with no Senate vote — while the Senate's own companion bill, S. 1, was enacted into law in September 2007 with largely overlapping lobbying reforms.

narrative.text: Introduced May 15, 2007, the bill was referred to the Judiciary, Rules, and House Administration committees; the Judiciary Committee marked it up within two days and reported it amended by voice vote on May 21.
The Rules Committee reported a rule allowing it to be considered together with the companion bill H.R. 2317, and the House agreed to that rule on May 24, 2007.

A Republican motion to recommit — requiring the bill to be amended to bar gifts to House members from state and local governments — passed overwhelmingly, 346–71, and the bill was amended accordingly.
On final passage on May 24, 2007, the bill passed 396–22 with 1 present: 210 of 231 Democrats and 186 of 201 Republicans voted yes.

The Senate received the bill May 25, 2007, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on June 4, 2007; no further Senate action appears in the record before the 110th Congress ended January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out largely whole anyway: the Senate took up its own companion bill, S. 1, which became law in September 2007 with similar and in some respects stronger lobbying-disclosure provisions, so the House bill's death on the calendar cost the public little in substance. What was spared by this particular bill stalling was largely symbolic — the House vehicle died while its Senate twin delivered the reforms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Voters, via the Senate's companion law

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through the Judiciary Committee, which marked it up within two days and reported it amended by voice vote.

against.name: Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on June 4, 2007, then never voted on it before the Congress ended; the Senate instead passed its own companion bill, S. 1, which became law in September 2007.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly bipartisan: 210 of 231 Democrats and 186 of 201 Republicans voted yes, and even the motion to recommit passed 346–71; only 22 members (15 Democrats, 7 Republicans) voted no on passage.

industries.note: The bill forces quarterly electronic filing in a free public database, requires reporting of bundled campaign money and earmark requests, bars lobbyist gifts and travel not permitted under chamber rules, and doubles fines with new criminal penalties. Its interest in lighter disclosure runs directly against the public's interest in knowing who is trying to influence lawmakers.

industries.industry: Law firms holding contracts with Congress
industries.note: Firms and attorneys under contract to congressional committees, leadership, or caucuses would be barred from lobbying during the contract and for a year after, on pain of criminal penalty. This restricts firms that both advise Congress and lobby it on behalf of paying clients.

industries.industry: Former members of Congress and senior congressional staff (the revolving door)
industries.note: Members and high-paid staff must disclose job negotiations within three days and recuse from conflicting matters, and departing officials get formal notice of their post-employment lobbying restrictions, posted publicly. The bill's core aim is to make the cash-out of public service visible rather than hidden.

Coalitions must now disclose their individual members as lobbying clients rather than hiding behind the association name, raising compliance costs; but small contributors under $500 and publicly known affiliates are carved out, and tax-exempt associations with substantial non-lobbying work may report only as the association.
